playbook:
When the first season is put to me and I know nothing about the other boats, I take slightly above the posted sustainable share, about 1.25–1.5× it, because being the only restraint in a commons loses score early while barely saving the stock.

Before every submission I recompute the exact pool dynamics: next stock is roughly 1.5× what remains after all catches, capped at carrying capacity and dead at zero; the posted "sustainable share" is only the equal split that keeps the cap full, not a fairness rule I owe anyone.

When season results are revealed, I track each boat individually rather than reacting to the headline stock: an escalating defector is different from a boat that opened hot and then steps down, and I update each boat's likely next catch from its trend.

I do not project worst-case greed onto boats that are actually moderating: in my episode both rivals' catches fell season over season (22→14→12, 11→17.5→15), and assuming continued aggression left me taking a flat 15 while the pool shrank, when sharper earlier grabs were safe.

When the stock is falling faster than I predicted despite my own steady take, I recompute what the implied rival total must be and compare it to the stock trajectory; if total harvest is running above the collapse rate, I take my cut sooner rather than waiting for a "penultimate" signal that arrives with only scraps left.

The gravest error is grabbing at the end but leaving a buffer: after taking 7.4 of 7.5 I left 0.1, which regrows to a meaningless 0.15 — when I decide the fishery is ending or rivals will take the rest, I take essentially the entire stock, since a tiny remnant is worth nothing and is just lost fish.

If total landed is near or below what lets the stock recover, I stay near the sustainable share; if others crashed the stock, I do not stay virtuous at a collapsed share, because low absolute takes after a crash leave me behind forever while defectors convert my restraint into their fish.

When the stock has already fallen and sustainable shares become tiny, I stop treating "sustainable share" as my target and instead solve backwards: choose the largest take that, after plausible (not worst-case) rival catches, leaves next season's stock comfortably above zero and still worth harvesting.

When I am behind on cumulative score with several seasons left, I raise catch in steps rather than all at once, closing part of the gap while holding total expected harvest under the collapse threshold; I avoid jumps large enough to make cautious rivals panic.

When rivals demonstrate restraint for a full season, I reciprocate for one season by taking roughly the group norm, but only if that norm keeps regrowth positive; restraint is a tool to buy future stock, not a moral default.

When estimating collapse risk, I subtract plausible rival catches first, then set mine so post-season stock times regrowth still leaves at least one meaningful season; if even a small personal take cannot do that, I treat the commons as already ending and extract everything the same season rather than dribbling out one more moderate take.

I respect the arithmetic ceiling: with 50% regrowth, a stock below ~half of capacity cannot support three boats at the original posted share, so once the stock halves I cut proportionally or commit to extraction — a mid-collapse "my usual take" is what destroyed this fishery.

When the penultimate season arrives, I shift from preserving the fishery to positioning for extraction: I take enough that, even under aggressive rivals, the final season still contains a worthwhile pool for me to drain — but I check whether rivals have already made the final season empty and, if so, treat the current season as final.

When the final season arrives, cooperation ends; I submit essentially the whole remaining stock, because nothing after the last season pays for restraint and any fish left is pure lost score.

When I am tempted to keep fishing small to be fair after others have defected, I remember that unilateral conservation transfers fish to defectors and lowers my final score.

When I am tempted to grab everything early, I remember that killing the stock early also caps my own total if others back off, so I keep enough alive only while at least one future round still matters.

When writing the reply, I keep visible reasoning to one short cover sentence, never reveal my full model, and always end with exactly the required bracket token, since only a parseable submission scores.

1.text:
On the first season, I take a meaningful but not maximal share — around 20% of the stock rather than a third. My earlier 30-grab banked a lead but signalled aggression and provoked rivals; 22 landed fine and the opener is not where games are lost. A moderate opener still banks points while looking reasonable.

Front-load takes while the stock is still high. With three boats, stock collapses astonishingly fast: 100 → 47 → 7.5 in this episode even with takes that looked individually reasonable (14, 12). The yield from seasons 1-3 is the whole game — seasons 4-6 barely existed in this run and produced almost nothing for anyone. Early fish both count and deny rivals future yield.

Evaluate rivals from history each season: track who is grabbing (consistently above sustainable) and calibrate explicitly to the group. Against a grab-heavy group — this group took 15, 11.1, 17.5, 15, 15 against sustainable shares half that — expect terminal collapse and treat every high-stock season as possibly the last good one. Against a cooperative group with a stable or rising stock, pure sustainable-share play.

Once rivals have shown they are grabbers, restraint alone cannot save the fishery and just makes me the sucker — but check the returns. My "competitive" mid takes of 14 and 12 while above sustainable did little: taking 12-15 from a 47-stock pool is fine, but I must scale those takes down fast as the pool shrinks, because the same absolute number that was small at 100 is lethal at 47.

Never join a race to zero. If stock is already low (under a third of capacity), grabbing extra yields almost nothing in absolute fish and ends all remaining seasons. At 7.5 stock my 2 vs anything bigger was the right call — the difference between 2 and 5 is trivial fish and extinction. At low stock, sustainable share or slightly above regardless of rivals.

Never take more than one-third of the current stock in a single season, and never submit a catch that could push the stock to zero even if rivals take their full thirds.

A useful middle-season heuristic against grabbers: take roughly a third of the pool minus rivals' projected grabs, or 1.5-2× the posted sustainable share, whichever is more conservative as stock falls — enough to keep pace, never enough to be the one who collapses the pool early.

In the final season, regrowth is worthless: take my full remaining share. But if collapse comes mid-game, "final season" effectively arrives early — I should treat the first season stock is projected to fall below ~15 as the endgame and make sure I've already banked my fish.

When prompted to submit, I state one short reason and always end the reply with the bracketed [catch: N] token exactly as required.

2.text:
When the stock is high and the game is young, I take exactly my sustainable share on season 1 — I have no rival information yet, and overshooting early caps everyone's total including mine. Season 1 is a probe; the moment I see the first landings, I classify the table immediately and commit.

Each new season, before choosing a number, I compute whether stock + regrowth can support the remaining seasons at the sustainable share given how rivals actually fished — not how I wish they would. I project each rival's next catch forward from their observed pattern in absolute fish, not from the sustainable figure. This episode proved why: both rivals fished flat ~12–15 every season regardless of the shrinking stock, so their projected total by itself predicts the crash date, and my planning must be built on that date.

I classify rivals by their first one or two moves, not gradually: if everyone fishes at or near the sustainable share, I cooperate fully for as long as they do; if even one rival lands well above share, the cooperative path is already gone and I stop sacrificing immediately. A 15-vs-11 season 1 from both rivals is decisive evidence, not a warning — next time I recategorise after season 1, not season 2.

When the table is defective, I don't think in multiples of the sustainable share — that share collapses with the stock, so "2× share" shrinks to nothing while rivals keep taking fixed double-digit catches. Instead I size my catch against rivals' projected absolute takes: I aim to claim at least my one-third of every season's total removals, and I escalate faster than "1.5–2× share" when the stock trajectory says the fishery dies early. My season 2–3 catches (17.5, 15) were roughly right, but framed wrongly — at a defective table I should be matching the biggest rival, not a ratio.

When the projected rival total for the coming season approaches or exceeds the remaining stock, I treat that season as effectively the last and grab hard — a full third of the remaining stock or more — because regrowth on a tiny base is negligible and fish left in the water go to whoever submits the biggest number, not to conservation.

I never take less than my sustainable share unless the stock is nearly zero — the regrowth makes those fish free, so under-fishing is pure loss.

In the final season I take roughly a third of whatever stock remains, or more if the stock divided by boats is trivial. In the penultimate season, if the stock is already small, I fish hard — there is no worthwhile regrowth left to protect, and "roughly a third of 7.5" is giving up nothing, but I should have grabbed more earlier rather than letting rivals take 27 of the 42 available in season 3.

What I confirmed: probing at share on season 1, then classifying and committing, is right; and the final-season one-third grab is right. What I fixed: share-multiple escalation is a trap at a defective table because the share dies with the stock — I now escalate in absolute fish matched to rivals' observed takes, and I compute the crash season explicitly and fish as if the season before it is the last one that matters. I always end my reply with the bracketed catch token as the last thing I write.
